Daniel 1.audience: Daniel and his friends are taken to Babylon in the third year of Jehoiakim (Daniel 1:1), around 605 BC. The book was read by Jews living under foreign rule.

culture.title: Training at court
culture.text: Young nobles from conquered nations were trained for three years in the language and learning of the Chaldeans—cuneiform writing, omens, astronomy—to serve the king.

culture.title: New names
culture.text: The young men receive Babylonian names, several honoring Babylonian gods: Belteshazzar (Bel), Abednego (Nebo).

culture.title: The king's meat
culture.text: The king's food would include meat not prepared according to the law and offered to Babylonian gods.

Daniel 2.audience: Nebuchadnezzar demands that his wise men tell him his dream and its meaning. From Daniel 2:4 to 7:28 the book is written in Aramaic.

culture.title: Chaldean wise men
culture.text: Magicians, astrologers, sorcerers, and Chaldeans served the Babylonian court, interpreting dreams and omens. Babylonian dream-omen books survive.

culture.title: A statue of metals
culture.text: Gold, silver, brass, iron, and clay—a sequence of declining metals also known from Greek writers such as Hesiod.

Daniel 3.audience: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego refuse to bow to Nebuchadnezzar's golden image. Hebrews 11:34 recalls those who "quenched the violence of fire."

culture.title: The plain of Dura
culture.text: The image was sixty cubits high and six wide (about 90 by 9 feet), perhaps a statue on a tall base.

culture.title: The royal orchestra
culture.text: Cornet, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery, and dulcimer. Three of these instrument names are Greek words.

culture.title: A furnace
culture.text: Brick kilns were common in Babylon. Jeremiah mentions Nebuchadnezzar burning two men (Jeremiah 29:22).

Daniel 4.audience: This chapter is written as Nebuchadnezzar's own proclamation to all peoples (Daniel 4:1), telling of his madness and restoration.

culture.title: Great Babylon
culture.text: "Is not this great Babylon, that I have built?" Nebuchadnezzar rebuilt Babylon on a grand scale; bricks stamped with his name have been found by the thousands.

culture.title: Eating grass like oxen
culture.text: Nebuchadnezzar lives in the field, eats grass, and grows long hair and nails until his reason returns.

Daniel 5.audience: Belshazzar holds a feast with the temple vessels on the night Babylon falls to the Medes and Persians (Daniel 5:30–31), in 539 BC.

culture.title: Belshazzar
culture.text: Babylonian texts show Belshazzar was the son of Nabonidus and ruled in Babylon while his father stayed in Arabia. That is why Daniel is offered the place of "third ruler" (Daniel 5:7).

culture.title: Writing on the plaster
culture.text: Palace walls were plastered and often painted, giving a smooth surface for the writing.

culture.title: Mene, Mene, Tekel, Upharsin
culture.text: The words are Aramaic weights—mina, shekel, and half-minas—and Daniel reads them as numbered, weighed, and divided.

Daniel 6.audience: Under Darius the Mede, Daniel keeps praying toward Jerusalem three times a day and is thrown into the lions' den (Daniel 6:10, 16).

culture.title: Unchangeable law
culture.text: "The law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not"—a royal decree could not be revoked (Esther 8:8).

culture.title: Praying toward Jerusalem
culture.text: Daniel prays at open windows toward Jerusalem, as Solomon had asked (1 Kings 8:48).

culture.title: Lions kept by kings
culture.text: Assyrian and Babylonian kings kept lions for royal hunts.

Daniel 7.audience: In the first year of Belshazzar, Daniel sees four beasts rise from the sea and "one like the Son of man" receive an everlasting kingdom (Daniel 7:1, 13–14). Jesus used this title of himself at his trial (Mark 14:62).

culture.title: Winged beasts
culture.text: A lion with eagle's wings resembles the winged lions on Babylonian and Assyrian palace walls.

culture.title: The Ancient of days
culture.text: God is pictured as a judge on a fiery throne with white garments and hair like wool.

Daniel 8.audience: In Belshazzar's third year, Daniel sees a ram and a goat. The angel explains them as Media and Persia and Grecia (Daniel 8:20–21). The text returns to Hebrew from here.

culture.title: Shushan by the Ulai
culture.text: In the vision Daniel is at Shushan (Susa) by the river Ulai, later a Persian royal capital.

culture.title: The great horn broken
culture.text: Alexander the Great died young in 323 BC, and his empire was divided among four of his generals.

Daniel 9.audience: In the first year of Darius, Daniel reads Jeremiah's prophecy of seventy years (Jeremiah 25:11) and prays a long confession for his people (Daniel 9:2–19).

culture.title: Reading the books
culture.text: Daniel learns "by books"—written scrolls of Jeremiah's prophecies that the exiles possessed.

culture.title: Sackcloth and ashes
culture.text: Fasting in sackcloth and ashes was the posture of national repentance.

culture.title: The evening oblation
culture.text: Gabriel comes "about the time of the evening oblation," the hour of the afternoon offering, even though the temple lay in ruins.

Daniel 10.audience: In the third year of Cyrus, after three weeks of mourning, Daniel sees a vision by the river Hiddekel (Tigris) (Daniel 10:1–4).

culture.title: A partial fast
culture.text: Daniel ate "no pleasant bread," meat, or wine and did not anoint himself for three weeks.

culture.title: Gold of Uphaz
culture.text: The man in the vision wears linen and a belt of fine gold of Uphaz, as in Jeremiah 10:9.

Daniel 11.audience: A detailed prophecy of the kings of the north and south. Historians identify these with the Seleucid kings of Syria and the Ptolemaic kings of Egypt who fought over Judea after Alexander.

culture.title: Ships of Chittim
culture.text: In 168 BC a Roman envoy, Popilius Laenas, forced the Seleucid king Antiochus IV to leave Egypt—ships from the west ("Chittim").

culture.title: The abomination that maketh desolate
culture.text: In 167 BC Antiochus IV set up a pagan altar in the temple and stopped the daily sacrifice (1 Maccabees 1:54). Jesus later spoke of "the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel" (Matthew 24:15).

Daniel 12.audience: The book ends with Michael standing for Daniel's people, the resurrection of "many of them that sleep in the dust" (Daniel 12:2), and Daniel told to seal the book.

culture.title: Sealing the book
culture.text: Important documents were sealed to preserve them unaltered until the proper time (compare Jeremiah 32:14).

culture.title: Shining as the stars
culture.text: The wise "shall shine as the brightness of the firmament"—Jesus uses similar words (Matthew 13:43).
